intro: This branch is about limits: what value a calculation is heading toward as its input gets closer and closer to some number. Limits are the foundation that the rest of calculus is built on.

VI.1.01.what: A limit is the value something heads toward as you get closer and closer, even if it never quite arrives. Think of walking halfway to a wall, again and again.

levels.a: Describes in words what it means for a quantity to approach a value.
levels.b: Explains that where a formula is heading can differ from its actual value there.
levels.c: Reads and writes the standard shorthand for a limit.
levels.d: Uses limits to untangle Zeno's paradox of halving the distance forever.

VI.1.02.what: Guessing a limit by making a table of values that creep closer and closer to the point of interest.

levels.a: Builds a table of values for inputs getting close to a chosen number.
levels.b: Approaches the number from both below and above in the table.
levels.c: Reads the trend in the table to estimate the limit.
levels.d: Recognizes cases where a table gives a misleading answer and explains why.

VI.1.03.what: Finding a limit by looking at a graph and following the curve toward a point.

levels.a: Traces a curve with a finger to see what height it approaches.
levels.b: Finds limits at a point where the graph has a hole.
levels.c: Reads graphs with jumps, where the two sides head to different heights.
levels.d: Explains that the limit ignores whatever happens exactly at the point itself.

VI.1.04.what: Looking at the approach from just one side, the left or the right, and comparing the two.

levels.a: Finds the value approached when coming from the left only.
levels.b: Finds the value approached when coming from the right only.
levels.c: Explains that a full limit exists only when both sides agree.
levels.d: Finds one-sided limits for functions defined by different rules on different pieces.

VI.1.05.what: Recognizing situations where a limit simply does not exist, and saying why.

levels.a: Spots a jump in a graph as a reason a limit fails.
levels.b: Spots values shooting off to infinity as a reason a limit fails.
levels.c: Spots endless wiggling, faster and faster, as a reason a limit fails.
levels.d: Explains in words exactly why a given limit does not exist.

VI.1.06.what: Rules that let you break a complicated limit into simpler limits and combine the answers.

levels.a: Finds the limit of a sum or difference from the separate limits.
levels.b: Finds the limit of a product or quotient from the separate limits.
levels.c: Handles powers and roots of expressions with known limits.
levels.d: Uses the rules one careful step at a time, naming each rule used.

VI.1.07.what: The simplest way to find a limit: just plug the number in, when that is allowed.

levels.a: Recognizes when plugging the number straight in gives the right answer.
levels.b: Plugs in to find limits of polynomials and fractions made of polynomials.
levels.c: Recognizes that getting zero over zero means more work is needed.
levels.d: Recognizes that a nonzero number over zero means the values blow up.

VI.1.08.what: When plugging in gives zero over zero, factoring the top and bottom and canceling the troublemaker often reveals the limit.

levels.a: Factors the top and bottom of a fraction.
levels.b: Cancels the common factor that caused the zero over zero.
levels.c: Plugs in the number to the simplified expression to find the limit.
levels.d: Explains why canceling is allowed even though that input was a problem.

VI.1.09.what: A trick for limits with square roots: multiply by a matching partner expression to clear the root out of the way.

levels.a: Multiplies top and bottom by the partner with the opposite sign (the conjugate).
levels.b: Simplifies the result, which removes the square root from one part.
levels.c: Cancels the factor that was causing zero over zero.
levels.d: Plugs in the number to finish the limit.

VI.1.10.what: Finding limits of fractions that have smaller fractions stacked inside them.

levels.a: Combines the small fractions into one over a common bottom.
levels.b: Simplifies the stacked fraction into a single fraction.
levels.c: Cancels the factor that was causing zero over zero.
levels.d: Plugs in the number to finish the limit.

VI.1.11.what: The squeeze theorem: if something is trapped between two things heading to the same value, it must head there too.

levels.a: Explains the squeeze idea with a picture of one curve trapped between two others.
levels.b: Finds two simpler expressions that trap the tricky one.
levels.c: Squeezes a wiggling expression, like x squared times sine of one over x.
levels.d: Writes out a complete squeeze argument in clear sentences.

VI.1.12.what: Two famous limits involving sine and cosine near zero, which are needed later for the derivatives of trig functions.

levels.a: Uses the fact that sine of x divided by x approaches 1 near zero.
levels.b: Uses the fact that one minus cosine x, divided by x, approaches 0.
levels.c: Adjusts for a scaled angle, such as sine of 3x over x.
levels.d: Follows and explains a proof of the sine limit using a circle diagram.

VI.1.13.what: Describing values that grow without end near a point, like dividing by a number shrinking toward zero.

levels.a: Recognizes when values grow without bound near a point.
levels.b: Decides whether values head to plus or minus infinity from each side.
levels.c: Finds the vertical lines (asymptotes) that a graph shoots up or down beside.
levels.d: Writes these results using correct limit notation with infinity.

VI.1.14.what: Asking what happens to a formula as the input gets huge, in either the positive or negative direction.

levels.a: Describes where a function is heading as x becomes very large or very negative.
levels.b: Divides top and bottom by the biggest power of x to find the limit.
levels.c: Compares how fast exponentials and logarithms grow for huge inputs.
levels.d: Handles limits at infinity that involve square roots.

VI.1.15.what: Using limits at infinity to find the flat lines a graph settles toward far out to the left or right.

levels.a: Finds the level a fraction settles to by comparing the highest powers.
levels.b: Handles graphs that settle to different levels on the left and right ends.
levels.c: Recognizes graphs that wiggle back and forth across their settling level.
levels.d: Sketches a graph showing its long-run flat lines.

VI.1.16.what: A function is continuous at a point if its graph passes through without a break. Informally, you can draw it without lifting your pencil.

levels.a: Checks that the function actually has a value at the point.
levels.b: Checks that the limit at the point exists.
levels.c: Checks that the value and the limit are equal, completing the test.
levels.d: Decides whether a function is continuous over a whole stretch of inputs.

VI.1.17.what: Naming the different ways a graph can break: a single missing point, a jump, or a shoot-off to infinity.

levels.a: Identifies a removable break, where just one point is missing or misplaced.
levels.b: Identifies a jump, where the graph leaps to a new height.
levels.c: Identifies an infinite break, where the graph shoots off near a vertical line.
levels.d: Classifies the type of break from the formula alone, without a graph.

VI.1.18.what: Adjusting a function so its graph has no breaks, by filling a hole or choosing the right numbers.

levels.a: Fills a hole by defining the missing value as the limit.
levels.b: Chooses a constant so the two pieces of a split function meet up.
levels.c: Chooses two constants at once so several pieces all join smoothly.
levels.d: Checks carefully that the adjusted function is now continuous.

VI.1.19.what: The intermediate value theorem: an unbroken curve going from below a height to above it must cross that height somewhere.

levels.a: States the theorem in plain words.
levels.b: Uses it to show an equation has a solution between two numbers.
levels.c: Explains why the theorem fails if the function has a break.
levels.d: Uses repeated halving (bisection) to close in on a solution.

VI.1.20.what: The fully precise definition of a limit, using two small tolerances called epsilon and delta. It turns "gets close" into a checkable promise.

levels.a: Explains the precise definition in everyday words.
levels.b: Finds how close the input must be for a straight-line function.
levels.c: Does the same for a squared function, where it takes more care.
levels.d: Writes a full formal proof that a limit has a certain value.
